title: CT logs as an unlabelled corpus for crash and divergence hunting
description:
## Why

Millions of real-world certificates. Not labelled, so not ground truth, and not a conformance suite -- but the largest untapped source of shapes no corpus author invented. The method is to run three oracles over a sample and investigate every disagreement, which is the pkix-difftest design already.

PKITS and x509-limbo already cover specified behaviour well (limbo has zero pkix-path false-reject bugs left once p384 is on). The unexplored territory is real-world weirdness, and this is where it lives.

## Availability -- VERIFIED 2026-11-27

* No canonical public corpus to download. You crawl.
* RFC 6962 get-entries is the classic route; logs cap the batch size (one researcher measured 32 entries per request regardless of what was asked).
* Modern logs are static/tiled -- clients fetch tiles rather than calling get-entries. Filippo Valsorda has an archiver that packs a static log into zips of 2^24-entry subtrees; a 2018 DigiCert archive is ~61 GiB for ~90.8M entries.
* Scale: Google-tracked logs went from ~3B to >7.5B entries over 2019. Sampling is mandatory, not optional.
* Let's Encrypt has retired its RFC 6962 logs, so check which logs still serve get-entries before planning a crawl.

## What

1. A sampled fetcher (tiles where available) writing DER to a corpus directory. Out of tree -- this is harness input, not a repo fixture.
2. Run the existing three-oracle harness over it; bucket by verdict class as the limbo baseline does.
3. Triage: a panic or a hang is a bug outright; a verdict disagreement needs the same hand-classification the limbo baseline got.

## Note

Expect the dominant finding to be parse-level: real CAs emit encodings no test suite contains. That is the point.
